Maladaptive Strategies.value: repeatedly blame myself for what happened

Threat.value: I feel unsafe unless my back is against a wall where I can see the room
When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

issues.item: Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened
issues.explanation: The self-blame item is not clinically supported elsewhere in the profile. There are no Negative Appraisal or Memory items indicating guilt, responsibility, shame, or a trauma narrative that would make repeated self-blame coherent. With this formulation, the only strong cycle is Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies, so maladaptive strategies should plausibly function to manage current danger/safety concerns. Drug use and avoiding thinking fit that threat-management loop, but repeated self-blame instead implies an unrepresented negative-appraisal process and sits weakly with the rest of the selected items.

vignette: Kiet, a 31-year-old carpenter of South Eastern Asian descent, still remembers the sound of his own screams echoing off the police station walls. It's been two years since that fateful night, but the memory remains etched in his mind like an open wound. As he recounts the events leading up to his arrest and subsequent beating at the hands of officers, Kiet's eyes dart around the room, his gaze lingering on any potential exit points. He can't shake off the feeling of being trapped, which is why he always sits with his back against a wall - it's the only way he can feel even remotely safe. This constant sense of unease has led Kiet down a path of self-destruction. When the anxiety becomes too much to bear, he turns to drugs to numb the pain. It's not something he's proud of, but it's become his go-to coping mechanism. On days when he's working on a project and things aren't going according to plan, Kiet's mind starts racing with worst-case scenarios. Delays or setbacks are no longer just minor inconveniences; they're omens of impending doom. His inability to relax, even in the comfort of his own home, has started to take a toll on his marriage. His wife, once his rock, now feels like she's walking on eggshells around him. As Kiet ruminates about that fateful night, he can't help but blame himself for what happened. "If only I had cooperated," he tells himself, "maybe things wouldn't have escalated." This self-blame has become a constant refrain in his mind, making it difficult for him to focus on anything else. His work as a carpenter, once a source of pride and joy, now feels like a chore. He's started to avoid taking on new projects, fearing that he won't be able to complete them on time or to the best of his abilities. Kiet's increasing reliance on maladaptive strategies has only served to heighten his sense of threat. The more he uses drugs to cope with his anxiety, the more anxious he becomes about being caught or losing control. His inability to relax in safe environments has started to make him question his own perception of reality. What if he's misjudging the situation entirely? What if there really is something to be afraid of? As Kiet sits in his living room, surrounded by the familiar comforts of home, he still can't shake off the feeling that danger lurks just around the corner. His back against the wall, he surveys the room with a mix of paranoia and desperation. It's this toxic cycle of threat and maladaptive strategies that has finally brought him to seek help - not because he wants to overcome his demons, but because he's afraid of losing everything that truly matters to him: his marriage, his job, and maybe even himself.
